sentences.text: Martinectes was a large polycotylid plesiosaur measuring at least around 5 meters in length.
Two large specimens of Martinectes, catalogued as KUVP 40001 and 40002, were collected from the Pierre Shale of Wyoming.
In 1997, Adams officially described these specimens as a new species of Trinacromerum, naming it T. bonneri.
Later, in 2008, O'Keefe demonstrated that Trinacromerum bonneri did not belong to Trinacromerum and assigned it to Dolichorhynchops.
Clark et al. found several characters distinguishing D. bonneri from the type species of Dolichorhynchops, establishing the new genus Martinectes for D. bonneri.
In 2023, Clark, O'Keefe, and Slack assigned Dolichorhynchops bonneri from the Sharon Springs Formation to the new genus Martinectes, meaning "Martin's swimmer".
In 2025, polycotylid teeth from the Rybushka Formation of European Russia were referred to cf. Martinectes.
In 2017, Everhart suggested that specimen KUVP 40001 could have measured up to 6 to 7 meters in length.
In 2025, Zverkov and Meleshin suggested Martinectes was around 5.5 meters long, similar to Polycotylus.
In 2026, Zhao estimated Martinectes measured 4.95 meters long and weighed 1.27 metric tons.
The genus Martinectes was described by Clark, O'Keefe, and Slack in 2023.
The type species of the genus Martinectes is Trinacromerum bonneri.
Martinectes bonneri was previously known as Trinacromerum bonneri and Dolichorhynchops bonneri.
Clark, O'Keefe, and Slack (2023) classified Martinectes as a polycotylid member of the clade Leptocleidia, sister to an unnamed polycotyline from the Niobrara Formation.
Martinectes, along with Dolichorhynchops species, forms the clade Dolichorhynchia within the Polycotylinae.
Martinectes belongs to the family Polycotylidae.
Martinectes belongs to the subfamily Polycotylinae.
The parent group of Martinectes is the clade Dolichorhynchia.
Martinectes is classified in the class Reptilia.
Martinectes lived between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago during the Campanian stage.
Martinectes lived during the Late Cretaceous (Campanian stage) in North America and possibly European Russia.
